RIYADH: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Saturday (Nov 21) that it had intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired towards Riyadh, marking the second Houthi attack on the Saudi capital in a few days, after its tallest skyscraper was struck on Thursday. A Reuters witness saw a projectile streak across the sky in Riyadh shortly before hearing a loud bang. The projectile left a trail of smoke in the sky. The latest attack followed an escalation in cross-border strikes on Friday, when the Saudi-led coalition said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah and carried out operations targeting Houthi missile and drone capabilities in the capital Sanaa. The Houthis threatened to target Saudi Red Sea ports, warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, and claimed attacks on a power station and port in southern Saudi Arabia.

The developments signalled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran. On Thursday, a Houthi attack damaged the Public Investment Fund tower , the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund and the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States, has been backing Yemen's internationally recognised government for more than a decade in a war that was fought to a stalemate in 2022 but reignited in July. The Houthis have seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and forced the Saudi-backed forces aligned with the government to retreat to defend their temporary capital in the southern port of Aden.

LAS VEGAS, Nov 20 : George Russell led a Mercedes one-two in a dry final practice session for the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Friday, after also setting the pace in Thursday night's rain-hit second practice. Russell, who won on the Strip circuit in 2024, lapped the 6.2-km street track in one minute, 34.041 seconds ahead of qualifying later on Friday. Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli was second, 0.911 seconds slower, with McLaren's Lando Norris third. Russell and Red Bull's Max Verstappen had a tense late-session exchange, running wheel-to-wheel after Verstappen overtook the Mercedes before slowing.

FAST

CARDIFF, Nov 20 : Lauren Price became the first Welsh boxer to become undisputed world champion when she beat bloodied Czech opponent Michaela Kotaskova by a unanimous points decision in a welterweight title fight in Cardiff on Friday. The 32-year-old 2020 Olympic middleweight champion added the vacant WBO welterweight belt to the WBA, WBC, IBO, Ring Magazine and IBF belts she already held. Price took her fight record to 11-0 and dealt Kotaskova, 35, her first defeat at welterweight. The outcome was never in doubt with the three judges each scoring the 10 round fight 100-90 to the home favourite, whose tall opponent had blood streaking down her face from a cut over her eye made worse by a later clash of heads.

In the closing seconds, Price had her hands above her head and was dancing out of reach as she celebrated before the bell. "As a professional everyone's dream is to become undisputed," said Price, after posing with her collection of belts in the ring. "I've ticked every accolade in boxing. I'm not finished. I've got many years left in me. But as far as tonight, it's all about the big fights now and it's all about my legacy." "I'd love to be boxing in a stadium in the summer, getting all of Wales behind me in the big fights. I'm undisputed at welterweight but I can move up." Promoter Ben Shalom called out undisputed and unbeaten heavyweight champion Claressa Shields as a future target. "Now we want Claressa Shields. We want her in Cardiff. Why not," he said ringside. "Come to Cardiff. Let's do a two-fight deal. One in the US, one in a stadium here in Cardiff. That's what we want. Lauren deserves to have the big fights here. "She will box in February, ideally in Cardiff and then we'll be in the stadium by June."

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 21 : Josh Hazlewood has backed Australia captain Pat Cummins and said he had no knowledge that sandpaper had been taken onto the field in a test against South Africa in 2018 as the renewed furore over the ball-tampering incident rumbled into a third week on Saturday.  The eight-year-old scandal reignited when former batsman Usman Khawaja said the whole team knew about the ball-tampering and not just the three players found culpable and sanctioned by Cricket Australia (CA)'s integrity unit. Khawaja has been backed by two of those punished - David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - while Hazlewood's fellow fast bowlers Mitch Starc and Cummins have maintained their stance that they knew nothing.  "We were interviewed straight after (the test) and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after," Hazlewood said in an interview in News Corp newspapers on Saturday.

"Two things stand out for me from what's been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? "The answer is no. When it boils down to it I think those two points are crucial." Cummins came under fire after his 68-minute news conference was followed by Bancroft, who was banned for nine months in 2018 for his use of sandpaper on the ball, releasing a 4,000-word statement on the incident.  Hazlewood addressed the allegations of complicity in Bancroft's account - that the use of sandpaper was widely discussed in the dressing room, that the opening batter asked the bowlers for feedback, and that he was congratulated by them for his work on the ball. Paceman Hazlewood, a noted exponent of the art of reverse swing, said the team at that time was split between bowlers and batters and they would have sat in different parts of the dressing room.  Like Cummins, he drew the distinction between roughing up one side of the ball and shining the other to allow for reverse swing, which is commonplace in cricket, and the use of sandpaper. "Looking after the ball is crucial in test cricket, especially in conditions like that, but he hasn't mentioned sandpaper, he hasn't mentioned taking something on the field," Hazlewood said.  "I have no doubt that he was asking us those things about the ball reversing. There's not one point in his statement where he says 'Oh, I'm doing this with sandpaper'." INDEPENDENT FORUM      CA attempted to draw a line under the revived scandal on Wednesday by announcing an independent forum for all the players to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 without fear of sanction. That the results of the forum would not be made public has been criticised by Warner, who with then-captain Steve Smith was banned for a year for his part in the scandal, and Khawaja with even the government weighing in with a call for transparency.  Meanwhile, pressure has intensified on Cummins to stand down as captain ahead of the four-test series against New Zealand starting next month.  "I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years, in particular as captain," Hazlewood said.  "He's a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response. "I think if we turned up for the first test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Source: Reuters

Nov 20 : GTCR is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments, the private equity group said in a filing on Friday, days after reports that a consortium effort with CD&R was dropped. Shares of Global Payments closed the day 10 per cent higher. It was up about 19 per cent so far in 2026. GTCR is working with other private equity firms to finance the potential deal, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. GTCR, which holds a 16.35 per cent stake in Global Payments and is the largest shareholder, said no definitive decision has been made. Global Payments did not immediately respond to Reuters request for a comment.

Private equity firms CD&R and GTCR had dropped their pursuit of Global Payments as a buyout consortium, Reuters reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter. The report had added that it was possible that CD&R and GTCR will resume the talks with Global Payments at a later date or another buyer for the company may emerge. Atlanta-based Global Payments is one of the world's largest payment processors. It enables merchants to accept card and digital payments and provides software and technology services to businesses. Its market value stood at about $22 billion, as of last close. The company has faced pressure in recent years from slowing growth in some business lines, intensifying competition and investor demands to boost profitability. Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover deal first and said it could value Global Payments at $50 billion, including debt and premium.

Nov 20 : Hackers this week breached a system that the US Department of Agriculture uses to send payments to farmers, NBC News reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter. The department notified employees of the incident on Thursday, the former officials told NBC. While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. It is not known who was responsible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the USDA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Source: Reuters

Shares of Oracle rose as much as 3.3 per cent in after-hours trading. • The comments follow investor scrutiny over the amount of capital Oracle would need to fund its expansion of AI data centers and its growing exposure to OpenAI • Oracle and OpenAI plan to develop 4.5 gigawatts of additional data-center capacity in the US, on top of the initial Stargate site in Abilene, Texas
